You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Review: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Enforcement Gaps

These are drafting issues that committee members, industry, advocates, or a court could raise. Some are clear gaps and some are judgment calls, so it's worth checking the legal interpretations with outside counsel or legislative experts before publishing.

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, so an operator could spread recovery across several vessels that each stay under the limit. Recovery from fixed platforms, seabed installations, or other non-vessel systems may not be covered at all.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "metric tons per year":** The bill doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry. Nodules hold a lot of water, so this could change the effective threshold substantially. "Per year" (calendar, fiscal, or rolling 12 months) is also undefined.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "seabed":** Neither term is defined. It's unclear whether collecting material on the seafloor without lifting it counts, and whether cutting into subsoil (as with sulfide deposits or cobalt crusts) counts as recovery "from the seabed."

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources":** Read literally, this could cover offshore oil, gas, or methane hydrates recovered below 200 meters. That would sweep far beyond the bill's apparent intent and invite a challenge or a narrowing interpretation.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), no geographic scope:** The definition doesn't say whether it covers the U.S. territorial sea, the EEZ, the continental shelf, areas beyond national jurisdiction, or all of these. This matters for both coverage and jurisdiction.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** "Secretary" is never defined, so it's unclear which department (Commerce? Interior?) has this authority.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B), open-ended delegation:** "Risks…comparable to" is a vague standard. No procedure (rulemaking, notice and comment) or criteria are specified. Because criminal penalties attach under Sec. 5(b), this invites vagueness and nondelegation challenges.

8. **Sec. 2(2), "corporation":** Only citizens and corporations are covered. LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entities (common structures for mining ventures) appear to fall outside the definition.

9. **Sec. 2(2), "organized under the laws of a State":** "State" is undefined, so entities organized in D.C., U.S. territories, or under federal law may be excluded. Lawful permanent residents are also excluded.

10. **Sec. 2(2), foreign subsidiaries:** There is no ownership or control test. A U.S. parent could conduct mining through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary, including one sponsored by another country at the International Seabed Authority (ISA).

11. **Sec. 2(3), covered vessel threshold:** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less are exempt from the registry even if they recover large volumes. "Equipped for the recovery" is undefined, so it's unclear whether a vessel must carry equipment at all times or whether gear can be swapped on and off.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

12. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States":** It's unclear whether this includes the EEZ and continental shelf. A foreign-flagged vessel operating in the U.S. EEZ might argue it is not "in the United States."

13. **Sec. 3(a), "person":** "Person" is never defined. This is relevant to whether foreign governments, state-owned enterprises, or federal entities are covered.

14. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in":** The phrase arguably covers only direct operators. Financing, chartering, supplying, processing, or importing minerals mined by others isn't addressed, and there is no import ban or anti-evasion clause.

15. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license":** The bill doesn't specify who must have issued the license. A license from NOAA, the ISA, or any foreign sponsoring state could arguably qualify. That makes the grandfather clause potentially very broad.

16. **Sec. 3(b), exploration vs. mining:** Exploration licenses (for example, under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act) authorize exploration, not commercial recovery. Exempting "mining conducted under" them creates ambiguity that a license holder could use to claim permission for commercial-scale recovery.

17. **Sec. 3(b), no limits on the grandfather clause:** Nothing addresses renewals, extensions, transfers, modifications, or expansion of grandfathered licenses. The exemption could last indefinitely and be sold to other operators.

18. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no tonnage cap, permit requirement, oversight, or reporting. Because the test is the activity's "purpose," large pilot or test mining could be labeled as assessment.

## Sec. 4: Registry

19. **Sec. 4(a), no deadline or penalty:** There is no deadline to register. Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report carries no penalty under this Act.

20. **Sec. 4(b), report contents:** The quarterly reports need not include tonnage, location, depth, or the wet/dry basis. Those are exactly the data needed to enforce the 10,000-ton threshold.

21. **Sec. 4(b), self-certification:** Reports are self-certified, with no verification, independent observers, vessel tracking (such as AIS or VMS requirements), audits, or inspection authority. False statements might reach 18 U.S.C. § 1001, but the bill creates no specific penalty.

22. **Sec. 4, no enforcement agency:** The bill doesn't name an agency to enforce the prohibition, such as NOAA or the Coast Guard. It grants no boarding, inspection, subpoena, or rulemaking authority, and doesn't say whether registry data is public.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

23. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, timing conflict:** Sec. 5(a) penalizes violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 makes the Act effective 180 days later. It's unclear whether conduct during that window is punishable, and applying penalties before the effective date raises fair-notice problems.

24. **Sec. 5(a), "each day":** A violation is defined by annual tonnage, so it's unclear when a violation "occurs." It could be the day the 10,000th ton is recovered, every day of that year, or only days after the threshold is crossed. It's also unclear whether tonnage recovered before the effective date counts toward the annual total.

25. **Sec. 5(a), missing enforcement mechanics:** The bill doesn't say who assesses penalties, what procedure or judicial review applies, or what factors set the amount. There is no injunctive relief, no forfeiture of vessels or recovered minerals, and no citizen-suit provision.

26. **Sec. 5(b), corporate fines:** "Fined under title 18" generally caps organizational felony fines at $500,000 under 18 U.S.C. § 3571, unless the alternative gain/loss fine applies. A criminal fine could therefore be far smaller than the civil penalty.

27. **Sec. 5(b), criminal liability tied to Sec. 2(1)(B):** Criminal liability can rest on conduct the Secretary later declares "comparable." This strengthens due process and vagueness challenges.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

28. **Sec. 6, "not later than 18 months":** It's unclear whether the State Department must start negotiating, or conclude an agreement, within 18 months. "Seek to negotiate" is hortatory and practically unenforceable either way. The section also doesn't address the ISA or the fact that the U.S. hasn't ratified UNCLOS.

## Sec. 7: Duration

29. **Sec. 7(a), joint resolution mechanism:** A joint resolution needs the President's signature and functions like an ordinary law, so this adds little beyond Congress's existing power to amend the Act. Nothing requires or funds the National Academies report or sets a timeline, and "serious harm" is undefined.

30. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), conflict:** Sec. 7(a) says the ban lasts "until" Congress acts, while Sec. 7(b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. The text doesn't reconcile the two. It's also unclear whether a joint resolution would end the ban everywhere or only for certain activities.

31. **Sec. 7(b), what ends at sunset:** The sunset terminates the entire Act, including the registry. It's unclear whether pending enforcement actions survive; the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) may help, but its application to expiring statutes is contestable. Also, the 10 years run from enactment while the Act takes effect 180 days later, so the ban effectively lasts about 9.5 years.

## Sec. 8 and Structural Gaps

32. **Sec. 8, 180-day window:** Operators could increase recovery before the effective date. Combined with item 23, the treatment of that period is unclear.

33. **Whole bill, relationship to existing law:** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or override the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), which authorizes NOAA to issue commercial recovery permits, or the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. This leaves conflicting authorities and invites litigation over which statute controls.

34. **Whole bill, no severability clause:** Without one, a successful challenge to a single provision (such as Sec. 2(1)(B)) could put the rest of the Act at risk.

35. **Whole bill, no regulatory authority:** No agency is directed or authorized to issue implementing regulations. This leaves undefined terms and measurement questions to be settled by enforcement actions and litigation.

For the markup, items 1, 8, 10, 15–18, 23, and 33 seem most likely to come up in debate or amendments. They're good candidates for questions to committee staff ahead of Thursday.
